newsitem.title: UK: Gas oil traders hit out at IPE futures pla.
newsitem.headline: Gas oil traders hit out at IPE futures pla.

text.p: European gas oil traders have slammed a duel being fought between two big trading houses on gas oil futures, saying the play has killed liquidity, distorted supply patterns and blunted the IPE's price discovery function.

Some infuriated traders called on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) to impose stiffer penalties on attempted squeezes. They warned that the IPE's status as the ultimate source of physical gas oil was at stake in what one player called a "battle of the giants" between two of Europe's main gas oil traders.
"Conditions are chaotic. It's ridiculous. There are huge supply hiccups. There are no barges available to move product into Germany and it's impossible to run a sensible hedge," one trader said.

Ironically, all the barges involved in the November physical delivery are tied up trying to shift a record 865,1000 tonnes of product around the ARA region while German end-users struggle with historically low winter stocks. Much oil in Germany is apparently moving into the heart of Germany on trucks, rather than the normal route up the Rhine.

"The IPE has to be much firmer. This is not in the interests of the market. Those in authority can correct the situation by not allowing these enormous squeezes. They don't do it in America because the penalties are so huge," said another trader in Germany late on Wednesday.

"I hope it will cost them (any party that is found to be in default) an awful a lot of money in order to discourage others from doing the same -- because there are a few other candidates who do it as well. "

The duel between Monte Carlo-based AIC, the main short, and the main long, Swiss-based Cargill International SA, on the November contract involves the bulk of the record 865,1000 tonnes delivery due between November 16-30 on the Rotterdam region barge market.
AIC says Cargill has been excessively slow to take delivery between November 16-20, the first of three five-day delivery periods which ended at midnight on Wednesday.
Cargill said late on Wednesday it was working with the IPE to ensure an orderly delivery in full compliance with the spirit and rules of the exchange.

Traders have said Cargill had established a large long position in November gas oil futures, betting that AIC, which has a large short position, would not be able to deliver into its commitments and therefore buy back its position at a higher price.

Barge trade has been extremely quiet for the past three days because the play has absorbed most barge capacity in ARA. The cargo market has also shrunk in part because those companies not involved in the play have prudently stayed on the sidelines.

Traders say the squeeze is the latest in a series that have frightened many trading houses out of the gas oil futures market, a relatively small and specialised market now usually worked only by a dozen trading houses.

One trader said the latest play was typical of a trend towards aggressive and inflexible conduct in settling physical deliveries, with two or three companies battling for advantage compared to a more gentlemanly procedure involving many more companies in earlier years.
"In the old days, if I could help someone I would, because next time it could be the other way around. We help each other -- because you meet each other more than once," one trader said.

"With the current situation apparently companies go for the throat, waving a book of IPE rules in one hand and a telephone to the counterparty in the other. It's not our way. I don't like it. and I don't want to be buried between two such competitors."
Another trader said: "Five years ago if there was a screen delivery, you had five, 10 or 20 delivering companies and the same number taking and all traders were involved. It was one big happy family.

"But pencils have been sharpened lately and what we see is that there are two sellers and one or two people picking up from the screen, and the others companies have withdrawn from that market because they see it is a battle of the giants.
"Nowadays I don't want to lift any product from the screen. We did it many times in the past but when there is such a huge delivery, it's always chaos and the product quality is always doubtful.

"I cannot sell the product from IPE to my clients. I prefer to buy refinery Rotterdam or Flushing or whatever. I pay a little bit above the screen, but that's not a problem, not problem I'm happy to pay it.
Asked to comment, IPE chief executive Lynton Jones said he was aware of such opinions.
"There are those allegations going around in the market and clearly if there is substance to them then we will be concerned about it," Jones added.

"Gas oil is a good contract, but it is a less liquid contract than Brent and there is always a potential problem in a contract with less liquidity, that these sorts of situations can arise. We would be concerned at the allegations if we felt it was damaging the gas oil contract."
